title: Delegation interfaces that keep people in meaningful control of computer work

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an interface through which a person can delegate an extended computer workflow while retaining effective authority over its execution. The person would specify the intended outcome and limits on the agent’s authority, inspect consequential decisions and progress, resolve ambiguity, interrupt or redirect work, and verify the result. Meaningful control would require these capabilities to work in practice: displaying a permission setting or providing a stop button would not by itself establish that a person understands or can influence what happens.

The central HCI contribution is the relationship between the person and the executing agent: how authority is expressed, when uncertainty is brought back to the person, what progress information is useful, and how mistakes are handled. Reliable memory, reasoning, tool use, and execution are enabling dependencies. The supplied benchmark identifies related technical needs, including maintaining task state, monitoring changing environments, checking final artifacts, and repairing errors across long workflows; it does not demonstrate an interface that provides meaningful human control.

A design concern is how to communicate enough information for informed supervision without making the person reconstruct every operation. Detailed click transcripts could impose excessive monitoring work, while a polished final summary could omit a consequential mistake. These are plausible interface risks motivating the proposal, but the supplied evidence does not test either claim or establish which presentation would best support users.

significance.text: Conditional significance: if effective supervision interfaces were combined with sufficiently reliable agents, people could interact with computers by assigning complex outcomes and intervening at meaningful decision points. Delegation could become a general interaction technique spanning applications. Its value would come from reducing the need to direct each operation while preserving the person’s ability to understand, authorize, and correct consequential work.

Possible downstream benefits include completing unfamiliar workflows with less operational expertise and managing longer tasks with less continuous attention. These benefits depend on whether supervision, clarification, and verification actually cost less effort than performing the work directly. Broad adoption, dependable operation across arbitrary applications, and benefits for different user populations remain possibilities requiring evidence. The proposal concerns supervised workflows; it does not establish that an agent can safely receive unrestricted authority or that all outcomes can be reversed.

The benchmark provides a concrete reason execution quality remains part of this challenge: agents can lose instruction constraints, overlook information encountered during execution, and proceed despite missing evidence that should prompt clarification. An understandable interface could help people detect or address such failures, but interface improvements alone have not been shown to eliminate them. The technical dependency is improved agent capability and reliability; the supplied evidence does not establish that larger models specifically are necessary.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved interface capability is dependable delegation with demonstrable human authority, understanding, intervention, and recovery over extended work. A system would need to turn a person’s intentions into actionable limits, recognize when the next decision exceeds those limits, and request clarification at a useful moment. It would also need to present changing state and consequential choices in a form that supports informed action without requiring continuous inspection. This is a synthesis of the proposed research target, not a demonstrated interface architecture.

The underlying execution barriers include preserving constraints and relevant information over long workflows, monitoring changes in applications, recognizing missing evidence, verifying final outputs, and repairing errors. These capabilities must remain coordinated as earlier actions change the environment and affect later decisions. The supplied benchmark documents failures that motivate these requirements, including missed instructions and inadequate use of the user channel when information is missing.

Proposed engineering requirements include connecting permission controls to actual execution, making interruption and redirection take effect before consequential actions occur, and exposing evidence that allows users to check outcomes. Recovery must distinguish actions that can be reversed from actions that require compensation or must be prevented. A useful research result would also establish when additional updates or questions improve control and when they merely add supervision work.

current_state.text: Agents already complete some computer tasks, with results depending on the benchmark and configuration. The supplied preprint, OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks, identifies XLANG Lab and Collaborators and names Mengqi Yuan, Zilong Zhou, and Xinzhuang Xiong as leading contributors. The reviewed text identifies arXiv:2606.29537v2, dated 13 July 2026. A 28 June 2026 submission date appears in the supplied metadata but was not independently confirmed in the retained document text.

Section 3 and Table 3 report 20.6% strict binary completion and a 54.8% partial score for the best reported configuration with a 500-step budget: Claude Opus 4.8 using maximum thinking and batched tool calls. Table averages cover 108 tasks. The partial score is a separate benchmark measure and should not be interpreted as full task completion. Other configurations perform differently, so this result describes a particular evaluation rather than a universal capability ceiling.

There is a small internal numerical inconsistency: nearby prose uses 20.5%, while Table 3, the main-results paragraph, abstract, and conclusion report 20.6%. The latter is retained here with its specific table and configuration attribution. The benchmark also documents execution and safety failures relevant to delegation, but it does not directly evaluate meaningful human control or establish that a particular supervision interface resolves those failures. Its simulated user does not replace a study of real participants’ understanding and intervention.

The result is reported in a preprint; the supplied material does not establish peer-reviewed confirmation or independent replication. The review had partial retained text, explicitly truncated in Appendix C.5, and no supplied figure images. The relevant results table and supporting prose were retained, so these access limitations do not by themselves undermine the scoped numerical attribution. The supplied search record is empty: coverage through 1 November 2026, the existence of newer results, and continued openness of the overall research target at that date cannot be established from these inputs.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independent participants would delegate long-running, unfamiliar workflows spanning several applications. They would set permissions, inspect concise decision-relevant state, resolve ambiguity, interrupt and redirect execution, and verify results or recover from errors. Comparisons with unaided users and existing agents would test whether delegation improves completed work while preserving effective control. These are proposed evaluation conditions, not an established completion standard.
completion_criteria.label: Delegation improves completed work while preserving effective user control

completion_criteria.text: The evaluation should measure consequential errors, actions outside granted authority, supervision time, clarification quality, participants’ understanding of consequential decisions, and successful intervention. Counting clarification requests alone would be insufficient: a question can appropriately prevent an error or unnecessarily interrupt work. Likewise, an available interruption control would need to be tested for whether users recognize the need to intervene and whether the system responds in time. Success thresholds should be specified before evaluation rather than inferred after observing results.
completion_criteria.label: Control outcomes and supervision costs measured against prespecified thresholds

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundary requirements include reporting task selection, application conditions, agent configuration, permissions, intervention opportunities, failures, and supervision costs sufficiently for independent repetition. Evaluation should distinguish successful reversal from compensation and prevention for irreversible outcomes. Repeated results across participants, tasks, applications, and changing conditions would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions; finite tests could not establish literal universality across computer work.
completion_criteria.label: Evaluation reporting enables independent repetition and establishes demonstrated boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: HCI-05, End-user programming that ordinary users can understand and maintain, has the closest stated overlap because both involve expressing intended behavior and understanding what a system will do. The intended distinction is that HCI-05 concerns authoring and maintaining software, whereas HCI-06 concerns supervising delegated execution. Only HCI-05’s title and the supplied editorial distinction are available, so the actual boundary between the full concepts remains unverified.

Roster-based comparison: HCI-04, An interface that makes inaccessible software operable through a user’s chosen modality, could overlap when delegation helps someone operate an application. Its stated focus is access through a chosen modality, while HCI-06 focuses on authority and supervision over delegated work. HCI-09, Privacy controls that remain understandable and enforceable across services, overlaps in understandable permissions and enforceable boundaries, with privacy as its specific concern. HCI-10, Lifelong personal memory augmentation with controllable evidence, overlaps in inspecting evidence and retaining context, while addressing long-term personal memory rather than execution of a delegated workflow.

Roster-based comparison: HCI-01, A predictive science of human–computer interaction, could inform testable accounts of supervision effort, understanding, and intervention. HCI-02, Reliable communication and computer control after profound paralysis, and HCI-08, Real-time conversational interfaces across signed and spoken languages, concern communication and control channels through which delegation might be accessed. Their stated goals remain distinct from controlling an agent’s extended work.

Roster-based comparison: HCI-03, A general-purpose, high-fidelity interface for touch and physical force, and HCI-07, Everyday visual computing with perceptually convincing spatial displays, concern sensory interaction capabilities that might host delegation interfaces without themselves establishing meaningful supervisory control. HCI-11, Remote collaboration with usable shared social and spatial cues, concerns collaboration between people; it could intersect with delegated work in shared settings. These relationships are conceptual inferences from the supplied titles, not findings from reviews of those entries.

unresolved_issues: Whether particular progress displays, transcripts, or summaries improve understanding and reduce supervision effort remains untested in the supplied evidence.
No supplied human-participant study establishes effective authority setting, timely intervention, or recovery for the proposed interface.
Concrete success thresholds, acceptable supervision costs, and practical application boundaries remain to be specified.
The source’s nearby 20.5% statement remains inconsistent with its repeated 20.6% result; no further resolution is supplied.
The June submission date is metadata-only, and peer-reviewed confirmation or independent replication is not established.
The empty search record prevents determining whether newer results existed or the overall capability remained unsolved by 1 November 2026.
Source access was partial, with Appendix C.5 truncated and figure images unavailable to the review.
Actual overlap with HCI-05 and other roster entries requires their full records; the supplied titles support only provisional comparisons.
